subject: math
domain: Algebra — Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
cluster: Understand solving equations as a process of reasoning
description: Students solve equations in one variable that contain rational expressions (a variable in a denominator) or radical expressions (a variable under a square or cube root), and they understand WHY an algebraically valid step can introduce a solution that does not satisfy the original equation. For rational equations they identify restricted values (denominators that cannot equal $0$), clear denominators by multiplying through by the LCD, solve the resulting polynomial equation, and reject any root that hits a restriction. For radical equations they isolate a radical, square (or cube) both sides, solve, and check each candidate, because squaring is not reversible and can create extraneous roots. Students explain how an extraneous solution arises (for example, multiplying by an expression that equals $0$, or squaring an equation where the two sides have opposite signs) and produce their own example demonstrating it. All answers are exact (fractions or simplified radicals), never rounded decimals.
subSkills: Identify the domain restrictions of a rational equation (values that make any denominator $0$) before solving
Find the least common denominator of a rational equation and multiply every term by it to clear fractions
Solve the resulting linear or quadratic equation and check each candidate against the domain restrictions, discarding extraneous roots
Isolate a single radical so that one side is exactly $\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}$ before raising both sides to a power
Square both sides of a radical equation (or cube for a cube root) and solve the resulting polynomial equation
Handle equations with two radicals by isolating, squaring, isolating the remaining radical, and squaring again
Substitute every candidate solution back into the ORIGINAL equation to confirm it is valid and reject extraneous ones
Explain the mechanism by which an extraneous solution arises (multiplying by a zero factor, or squaring sides of opposite sign) and construct an example that produces one

problemArchetypes.name: Single rational equation, proportion form
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\dfrac{3}{x-2}=\dfrac{5}{x+4}$. (Cross multiply: $3(x+4)=5(x-2)$, so $3x+12=5x-10$, $x=11$; $x=11$ violates no restriction, so it is valid.)

problemArchetypes.name: Rational equation with sum of fractions, clear the LCD
Rational equation whose candidate is extraneous (restricted value)
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\dfrac{x}{x-3}=\dfrac{3}{x-3}+2$. (Multiply by $x-3$: $x=3+2(x-3)$, giving $x=3$; but $x=3$ makes a denominator $0$, so it is extraneous and there is NO solution.)

problemArchetypes.name: Rational equation reducing to a quadratic
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x-2}=\dfrac{3}{4}$. (Multiply by $4x(x-2)$: $4(x-2)+4x=3x(x-2)$, so $3x^2-14x+8=0$, $(3x-2)(x-4)=0$, giving $x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ or $x=4$, both valid.)

problemArchetypes.name: Radical equation with a linear term to isolate first
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\sqrt{2x+3}-x=0$. (Isolate $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$, square: $2x+3=x^2$, so $x^2-2x-3=0$, $(x-3)(x+1)=0$; $x=3$ checks but $x=-1$ gives $\sqrt{1}=-1$ which is false, so $x=-1$ is extraneous and only $x=3$ is valid.)

problemArchetypes.name: Cube-root equation
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\sqrt[3]{2x-1}=3$. (Cube: $2x-1=27$, so $x=14$; cube roots never create extraneous solutions because cubing is one-to-one.)

problemArchetypes.name: Two-radical equation requiring squaring twice
problemArchetypes.example: Solve $\sqrt{x+7}-\sqrt{x}=1$. (Isolate $\sqrt{x+7}=1+\sqrt{x}$, square: $x+7=1+2\sqrt{x}+x$, so $\sqrt{x}=3$, then $x=9$; check valid.)

problemArchetypes.name: Construct/explain an extraneous solution
problemArchetypes.example: Give an example of a radical equation whose algebra yields a candidate that is NOT a solution, and explain why. (For instance $\sqrt{x}=-2$ leads to $x=4$ after squaring, but $\sqrt{4}=2\neq-2$; squaring erased the sign conflict.)

Easy.description: One-step-to-isolate problems that resolve to a single linear equation and a quick check. A rational equation in clean proportion form $\dfrac{a}{x+b}=\dfrac{c}{x+d}$ cross-multiplied to a linear equation, OR an already-isolated square/cube root set equal to a constant. The candidate is valid (no extraneous root) and the answer is a small integer or simple fraction. tier1 lives here through early Medium.
constraints: Rational form is a single proportion (one fraction equals one fraction) or one fraction equals a constant
Radical form is already isolated: $\sqrt{\text{linear}}=k$ or $\sqrt[3]{\text{linear}}=k$ with $k\ge0$ for square roots
Clearing the radical or denominator yields a LINEAR equation
The single candidate is valid; the check confirms it (no extraneous root introduced)
Coefficients and the answer are small integers or simple fractions

Medium.description: Two-step problems that require setting up the LCD across a sum of fractions or isolating a radical before squaring, and that turn on the extraneous-solution check. Includes rational equations summing two or three fractions, and radical equations of the form $\sqrt{ax+b}=x+c$ that square to a quadratic with two candidates where exactly one (or neither) survives the check. This is the central band of a typical solve.
constraints: Rational equation has a sum of two or three fractions cleared by an LCD, reducing to a linear or simple quadratic equation
Radical equation requires isolating the radical before squaring, then squaring to a quadratic
At least some items produce a quadratic with two candidates, exactly one of which is extraneous and must be rejected by the check
Includes at least one rational item whose only candidate hits a domain restriction, giving NO solution
Answers are integers or simple fractions; checks against the ORIGINAL equation are required

Hard.description: Multi-step problems: rational equations that reduce to a quadratic after multiplying by an LCD with two distinct factors, two-radical equations requiring squaring twice, and the reasoning tasks that ask the student to explain or construct an extraneous solution. The radical or rational structure is nested or doubled, and exact simplified radical/fraction answers are required.
constraints: Rational equation has an LCD with two distinct linear factors and reduces to a quadratic; both restrictions must be tracked
OR a two-radical equation $\sqrt{ax+b}\pm\sqrt{cx+d}=e$ requiring isolate-square-isolate-square
OR a radical equation whose answer is a simplified radical or fraction (not an integer)
OR an explain/construct task: produce an equation with an extraneous root and justify the mechanism (zero denominator or sign-conflict squaring)
Every candidate is checked in the original equation; exact values only, never rounded decimals

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accepts a candidate that makes a denominator zero, never checking domain restrictions
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\dfrac{x}{x-3}=\dfrac{3}{x-3}+2$ reports $x=3$ as the solution instead of recognizing it is extraneous and the equation has NO solution

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Believes squaring both sides can never create a false solution, so skips the check
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\sqrt{2x+3}=x$ reports both $x=3$ and $x=-1$, keeping $x=-1$ even though $\sqrt{1}=1\neq-1$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Squares term by term instead of squaring each whole side: treats $(a+\sqrt{b})^2$ as $a^2+b$
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\sqrt{x+7}=1+\sqrt{x}$ writes $x+7=1+x$ (dropping the $2\sqrt{x}$ cross term), concluding there is no solution instead of $x=9$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adds numerators over a common denominator incorrectly, or only multiplies SOME terms by the LCD
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{6}=\dfrac{1}{4}$ multiplies only the fraction terms by $12x$ and leaves the right side as $\dfrac{1}{4}$, getting $12+2x=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and a wrong answer

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Cross-multiplies a sum of fractions as if it were a single proportion
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{x-2}=\dfrac{3}{4}$ cross multiplies the left fractions directly to $4=3x(x-2)$ ignoring the $+$, producing the wrong quadratic

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Forgets that $\sqrt{\,\cdot\,}$ denotes the principal (non-negative) root, so accepts a negative radical value
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims $\sqrt{x}=-2$ has solution $x=4$, accepting it because squaring gives $4$, instead of stating there is NO solution

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Squares only one side or mishandles the constant when isolating, leaving the radical's effect uncleared
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\sqrt{x+5}=4$ writes $x+5=4$ (forgetting to square the right side) and reports $x=-1$ instead of $x=11$

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Confuses cube roots with square roots and looks for nonexistent extraneous roots, or rejects a valid negative radicand
commonMisconceptions.distractor: For $\sqrt[3]{2x-1}=3$ insists the radicand must be nonnegative or that a check is needed to discard a root, when cubing is one-to-one and $x=14$ is the unique valid solution
